overview.body:
**Tangaroa** (*tangaroa*) — Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing · God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa) — belongs to the Polynesian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing". The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)".

**Tangaroa** is ocean, sea creatures, fishing. The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)" and belongs to the polynesian tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Tangaroa** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/tangaroa/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *tangaroa* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in modern Polynesian orthographies; macron usage follows each tradition’s reference dictionaries. Etymologically the name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)".

The reconstructed proto-form is *Ta* (proto-polynesian, "God of the sea"). God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)

The ASCII form *tangaroa* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. Phoneme by phoneme:

- **tangaroa** — The canonical restored form Tangaroa.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: Say "tangaroa" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Tangaroa".

The ASCII form "tangaroa" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Tangaroa" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

The pronunciation given above reconstructs the sound world in which Tangaroa was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance prescription. The restoration Tangaroa keeps the prosodic information visible even when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

original-script.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual polynesian names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.

The form **Tangaroa** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

mythology.body:
The stories of Tangaroa place ocean, sea creatures, fishing at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Tangaroa appears in polynesian tradition as ocean, sea creatures, fishing. The name's meaning, "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Tangaroa in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Tangaroa survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Tangaroa gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

cultural-legacy.body:
Tangaroa remains a touchstone for understanding polynesian religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of Tangaroa includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Tangaroa remains findable and citable.

archaeology.body:
No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Tangaroa with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Polynesian name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Tangaroa, sanctuary or cult remains tied to ocean and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

meditation.body:
To contemplate Tangaroa is to hold the idea of ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing · God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa).

Sit with the restored form — Tangaroa — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *tangaroa* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.

oral-narratives.body:
Polynesian oral narratives, preserved in Māori, Hawaiian, Tahitian, and Rapa Nui traditions, recount the deeds and genealogies of Tangaroa. These stories were performed by specialists and recorded in the nineteenth century.

The restored form Tangaroa follows the orthographic conventions of the tradition.
